ENT Clinical Note

Subjective:
- Presenting complaint and trigger/exposure: Sudden-onset severe left-sided headache that woke patient at ~05:30 today; no clear external trigger identified.
- Symptom timeline and progression: Began early this morning, constant since onset; unchanged after paracetamol; slightly easier after lying down.
- ENT symptoms: 
  • Throat swelling/closure sensation – denied  
  • Voice change/hoarseness – denied  
  • Dysphagia/odynophagia – denied  
  • Drooling – denied  
  • Nasal/ocular symptoms – mild photophobia only; no rhinorrhoea, no tearing  
  • Stridor/noisy breathing – denied  
  • Dyspnea – denied  
  • Swelling (lips/tongue/uvula/face) – denied  
  • Ear pain/hearing changes – denied  
  • Neck pain/stiffness – denied  
- Relevant past episodes and treatments: History of intermittent, milder frontal headaches; no prior severe unilateral headache; no previous ED visits or injections for headache.
- Allergies and current medications:
  • Allergies – “None known.”  
  • Sertraline (dose/route/frequency not documented).  
  • Paracetamol taken once this morning (dose not documented).  
  • No other regular or rescue medications; no auto-injector devices.
- Any relevant social context: Lives with partner; significant work-related stress and late nights for ~2 months.

Objective:
- Observable swelling: None reported.
- Airway/breathing: Normal per history; no stridor or dyspnea.
- Mental status: Alert, oriented; no dizziness now; mood stable; denies self-harm thoughts.
- Vitals and examination findings: Not recorded (telephone consultation).
- Presence of another person: Partner at home (not present during call).

Assessment:
Working impression: New, severe unilateral headache most consistent with 1) Migraine without aura versus 2) Tension-type (stress-related) headache.

Evidence summary: Unilateral left pain, photophobia, poor response to paracetamol, stress/sleep-deprivation trigger, prior episodic headaches support migraine; prolonged work stress and history of anxiety support tension component; absence of red-flag neurological or ENT airway signs.

DDx reference (aligned with transcript):
1. Migraine without aura – high likelihood (features above); no vomiting or aura but these are not obligatory.
2. Tension-type headache – moderate likelihood (work stress, anxiety, prior similar frontal pain); opposing evidence: current unilateral focus and photophobia.
3. Subarachnoid haemorrhage – low but must not miss; sudden awakening and “worst headache” description; opposing evidence: normal conversational state, no neck stiffness, no neuro deficit. (Conflict noted: DDx flags low probability; transcript plan assumes benign etiology.)

Plan:
- Pharmacologic: Initiate ibuprofen (high-dose per current migraine guidelines; specific dose not documented in call) ± continue paracetamol as needed.
- Lifestyle / non-pharmacologic:
  • Encourage minimum 7–8 h sleep nightly.  
  • Maintain hydration ≥1.5–2 L non-caffeinated fluids daily.  
  • Recommend one-week self-certified leave from work to reduce stress.  
  • Provide self-referral link to local counselling service.
- Education / red-flags: Reviewed headache danger signs; advised to seek urgent care if sudden worsening pain, new neurological deficits, persistent vomiting, visual changes, neck stiffness, fever, altered consciousness, or any airway/breathing difficulties arise.
- Follow-up: Scheduled telephone follow-up in 1 week with GP service; earlier review if no improvement or any red-flags.
- ENT-specific: No airway compromise at present; no ENT intervention required. Monitor for any new ENT symptoms (voice change, swallowing difficulty, facial swelling) and seek immediate care if they develop.

Quality checks (document_quality):
● Missing but clinically expected elements: Exact ibuprofen dose/route/frequency; paracetamol dosing details; vital signs; full neurological examination; headache characteristics (quality, severity score, associated autonomic features); formal allergy list confirmation; ENT/airway exam findings.
● Conflicts between transcript and DDx: DDx lists cluster headache and cerebrovascular causes; transcript assessment emphasizes migraine/tension and does not arrange imaging—low-probability serious causes acknowledged but not actively worked up (conflict noted regarding SAH “must not miss”).
● Transcript quality: Clear audio, no significant inaudible sections; conversational but comprehensive history; no physical-exam data due to teleconsultation.
